title: Serving runtime — team wiki, runbooks, profiling & benchmarking playbook
author: Priya Desai
summary: Canonical team wiki page for the serving runtime: architecture overview, kernel & scheduling guidance, profiling playbook, benchmarking suite instructions, release note highlights, known issues, and primary runbooks for on-call.
content:
Overview:

This page is the canonical team wiki for Redwood's serving runtime. It collates architecture guidance, kernel/scheduling rules, profiling/playbook procedures, benchmarking suite usage, release-note highlights, and operational runbooks used by SRE and runtime engineers. Treat this as a reference — short how-tos are included along with links to deeper design docs and runbooks.

1) Runtime architecture (summary)

- Objective: provide a high-throughput, low-latency inference layer supporting continuous batching, KV cache reuse, quantization-friendly execution, and policy-based routing.
- Primary services and components:
  - runtime-controller: orchestration and request routing. Responsible for model routing, autoscale decisions, and canary rollout logic. (owned by eng-serving-runtime)
  - inference-workers: GPU-backed pods running the inference engine (intel/amd/nvidia variants by flavour).
  - kv-cache-service: shared Redis-backed prefix+KV cache for short-lived reuse across requests.
  - telemetry-proxy: aggregates tracing, token-level cost, and latency breakdowns to the Console.
- Data flow (high level): API -> runtime-controller -> scheduling -> inference-worker -> telemetry-proxy -> response.

Architectural constraints and SLOs:
- 99.9% p99 request latency < 600ms for hosted text-generation at 1k token seq on dedicated hardware profiles (r5-equivalent).
- Throughput SLO: maintain >= 95% of reserved throughput for Dedicated customers during business hours; burst policies allow short-term 150% throughput if capacity permits.
- Error budget and fallbacks: automatic fallback to lower-capacity model variant or neighboring-region routing when error budget exceeded for a model pool.

2) Kernel & scheduling guidance

- Scheduling goals: minimize tail latency, maximize GPU utilization, preserve model correctness (KV cache affinity), and avoid noisy-neighbor interference.
- Local scheduling policies:
  - affinity-by-customer: pin requests from the same customer/model-version to worker-local KV cache when possible.
  - max-batch-size: worker-specific; enforced by kernel-capacity config (see table below).
  - latency-first mode: used for latency-sensitive routes (e.g., interactive chat) — prioritizes small batches and preemptive scheduling.
  - throughput-first mode: used for async/large-batch jobs (embeddings pipelines) — emphasizes batch size and coalescing.

Quick reference scheduling table (config keys):

| config_key | description | example value | owner |
|-----------|-------------|---------------|-------|
| max_batch_size | Max tokens per kernel queue | 4096 | eng-serving-runtime |
| batch_timeout_ms | Max wait before dispatching partial batch | 8 | eng-serving-runtime |
| kv_affinity_ttl_ms | TTL for cached KV affinity | 300000 | eng-serving-runtime |
| scheduling_policy | latency|throughput|balanced | latency | runtime-controller |

Best practices:
- For low-latency routes: set batch_timeout_ms <= 10ms and max_batch_size capped to sequence-size*concurrency factor.
- For large-batch workloads: increase batch_timeout_ms to 30-50ms and allow max_batch_size to hit hardware concurrency peak.
- Avoid colocating large embedding workloads with low-latency chat on the same GPU pool. Use routing rules in runtime-controller to split traffic.

3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

Purpose: standardize profiling for perf regressions, hardware kernel tuning, and validation for new model onboards.

When to run:
1. New model/quantization profile introduced.
2. PRs touching kernel-selection, batching, or KV caching.
3. Elevated p99/p95 latency in production alert.

Procedure:
1) Reproduce the workload locally or in a staging cluster. Use the benchmarking harness (section 4):
   - ./bench/run_profile.sh --model <model-id> --seq 1024 --concurrency 8 --tokens_per_call 256
2) Capture traces: enable distributed tracing at debug level and collect a 10-minute window.
   - kctl exec -n runtime $(runtime-pod) -- /bin/sh -c 'export TRACE_LEVEL=debug; ./start-worker'
3) Kernel-level profiling: use nvprof/nsys (NVIDIA) or rocprof (AMD) on a staging worker.
   - nsys profile --output profile.nsys ./inference_worker --model <id> --loadtest 5000
4) CPU/GPU utilization and host metrics: capture with metrics-exporter; export to a csv for analysis.
5) Analyze hot paths: look for stalled dispatches, long memcpy, synchronization stalls, or high kernel launch overhead.
6) Tune and validate: adjust batch_timeout_ms, max_batch_size, or kernel selection heuristics. Re-run bench harness and confirm improvement.

Standard artifacts to attach to the ticket: profiling traces, kernel timeline screenshots, bench harness results (csv), and before/after SLO metrics.

4) Benchmarking suite (how-to)

Location: repos/bench and infra/bench-clusters (internal). Use the bench harness for both latency and throughput profiles.

Common commands:
- Latency profile: ./bench/latency_test.sh --model small-llama-v1 --seq 512 --concurrency 1 --runs 2000
- Throughput profile: ./bench/throughput_test.sh --model quant-30b --seq 1024 --concurrency 16 --duration 300
- End-to-end reproducible job (CI): ./bench/ci_run.sh --target perf/regression --thresholds perf-thresholds.yaml

Benchmark outputs and naming convention: bench-results/<model>/<date>/<run-id>.csv and bench-report/<model>/<date>/<run-id>.html

Metrics to collect (minimum):
- p50/p95/p99 latency (request + kernel)
- tokens/sec and GPU SM utilization
- memory high-watermark and page faults
- kernel occupancy and avg kernel launch latency

5) Release notes (serving runtime highlights)

- 2026-01-15: Runtime 3.2.0 
  - New: kernel-selection heuristic v2 (improves p99 on long seqs by ~18%).
  - Fix: memory leak in kv-cache-service for long-running streams.
  - Upgrade: default batch_timeout_ms lowered from 12ms -> 8ms for latency routes.

- 2025-11-02: Runtime 3.1.4
  - New: experimental AMD ROCm support for quantized 30B models.
  - Fix: race condition during worker shutdown causing inflight request loss.

6) Known issues (current and mitigations)

- Issue: p99 spikes when concurrent large-embedding jobs start on same pool.
  - Symptom: sudden p99 increase to >2s for unrelated small-seq routes.
  - Mitigation: runtime-controller policy to isolate embedding traffic; set scheduling_policy=throughput for embedding routes.

- Issue: intermittent NVMe read timeouts on cold-model fetches (rare).
  - Mitigation: pre-warm model caches during deploys; increase model-fetch timeout to 30s; track prefetch success rate.

- Issue: kernel-selection v2 may choose larger kernels on some custom-attention blocks causing increased memory transient.
  - Mitigation: guardrail in kernel-selector to fallback to v1 on OOM events; add model-specific overrides in model-onboarding.

7) Runtime runbooks (on-call)

Runbook: High p99 latency for hosted chat routes
- Pager: severity P1 if p99 > 1.5s for >5m across >=5% of requests.
- Owner: runtime-oncall (rotation: eng-sre + eng-serving-runtime)
- Steps:
  1. Check runtime-controller dashboards: request rate, p99, worker queue length.
  2. Identify noisy pools: filter by pool_id and customer. If a pool shows high SM usage (>90%) or queue depth > 1000, consider traffic shift.
  3. If noisy-tenant identified, apply routing rule: /api/v1/routes/<route>/override -> scheduling_policy=throughput or move to dedicated pool.
  4. If storage/model-fetch timeouts: check NVMe metrics and model fetch logs. Restart prefetch service if needed.
  5. If a kernel regression suspected: escalate to eng-serving-runtime and attach profiler artifacts.
  6. Post-incident: file an incident page under oncall-and-incident-response with timeline and remediation.

Runbook: Worker OOM or Crash Loop
- Pager: P0 if >10% workers in a pool are crash-looping for >3m.
- Steps:
  1. Review pod logs: kubectl -n runtime logs <pod> --previous
  2. Check OOM score and memory high-watermarks.
  3. If due to model size/quantization, update worker flavor to larger memory instance or use model-variant with lower-memory quantization.
  4. Roll back recent runtime release if crash correlates with a deployment.

8) Team wiki, ownership, and contacts

- Owners: eng-serving-runtime (primary), eng-sre (secondary).
- Primary contacts: Priya Desai (runtime lead), Michael Chen (performance), Sara Alvarez (oncall coordinator).
- Oncall schedule: see /team/oncall (linked page).

9) Troubleshooting checklist (fast triage)

- Confirm alert validity: compare to SLO/alert thresholds.
- Reproduce in staging with bench harness.
- Collect traces and kernel profiles (10 minutes window).
- Check recent rollouts: runtime-controller -> rollouts dashboard (last 60m).
- Apply mitigations (traffic-shift, worker restart, policy swap).

Appendices:
A. Example kernel tuning snippet (runtime-controller config yaml):

---
pools:
  - id: latency-prod-a
    scheduling_policy: latency
    max_batch_size: 2048
    batch_timeout_ms: 8
    kv_affinity_ttl_ms: 300000

B. Example bench command (full):
./bench/run_profile.sh --model redwood/small-llama-v1 --seq 1024 --concurrency 8 --tokens_per_call 256 --output bench-results/small-llama-v1/2026-02-10/run-01

C. Required artifacts for onboarding a new model:
- model-spec.yaml (name, arch, weights-uri, default-quantization)
- perf-report.csv (latency and throughput across hardware flavors)
- kernel-selection-report (nsys or rocprof output)
- security-scan results (if customer-provided weights)
